section_summary: This section assembles State Department, diplomatic, military, and naval reporting from 1938–1939 on alleged Japanese activity in Mexico, especially fishing fleets, immigration evasion, espionage, petroleum, mining, salt, construction, and commercial propaganda. It includes consular despatches from Guaymas and Mexicali, intelligence memoranda, cross-reference sheets, correspondence, press clippings, and a translated Japanese survey of Mexican politics and economic opportunities. Much of the material consists of unverified allegations or informant reporting reflecting contemporary American security concerns and anti-Japanese sentiment.

subfiles.title: Document file note on Japanese fishing and other activities in Mexican territorial waters
subfiles.about: The note refers to a despatch quoting Lawrence L. Berg on Japanese fishing and related activity in Mexican waters.
subfiles.summary: This indexing sheet points to related file numbers 894.20212/402 and 812.628/438. It identifies a June 7 Guaymas report containing quotations from Berg's June 4 letter.

subfiles.title: Document file note for Despatch No. 522 on Japanese vessel crews
subfiles.about: The note indexes a report about Japanese crews, Turtle Bay, and suspected smuggling into the United States.
subfiles.summary: It states that Japanese newcomers were allegedly shipped from a colony at Turtle Bay on American and Japanese fishing vessels operating from Los Angeles and San Diego. The note also frames Japanese labor as a threat to unemployed American fishermen.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese activities and fishing-vessel crews
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Yepis reports allegations that Japanese fishermen used the Turtle Bay colony and falsified shipping records to enter the United States.
subfiles.summary: The despatch alleges cooperation among Japanese organizers, Mexican agents, American shipmasters, ships' agents, and immigration or customs officials in moving Japanese crewmen through Mexican ports into the United States. It cites purported forged signatures and improperly issued seamen's identification cards and names T. Abie, James T. Shreve, Honest Muire, Arthur Homann, and P. B. McCaffrey. Yepis also presents strongly prejudicial claims about Japanese workers and argues that Japanese-backed fishing vessels displaced American labor. The WHITE EAGLE is described as nominally American-owned but effectively controlled by Japanese partners.

subfiles.title: File note on a Mexican fisheries commission to Todos Santos Bay
subfiles.about: The note records Japanese participation in a Mexican government commission studying Todos Santos Bay.
subfiles.summary: The commission included Japanese citizen Toshiye Yamashita and Japanese-born naturalized Mexican Salvador Meguro Yamasaki. The referenced despatch supplied information about the two men and commented on the commission's purpose.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division routing sheet
subfiles.to: Listed War, Navy, State, Commerce, and military attaché offices
subfiles.about: The sheet provides an internal distribution list for intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: It lists War Department branches, service arms, the Office of Naval Intelligence, State and Commerce Department divisions, and military attaché offices. The form allows recipients to retain, return, or forward the accompanying intelligence.

subfiles.title: Confidential memorandum on Japanese activities and Mexican political instability
subfiles.to: War Department and listed intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: The memorandum combines allegations of Japanese espionage with reporting about Gold Shirts and possible instability in the Cárdenas government.
subfiles.summary: It identifies Japanese ichthyologists Yoshichi Mitsui and T. Yamashita as suspected spies, calls the government-employed ichthyologist Osawa a spy, and alleges that Saito headed a Mexico City espionage ring. A second section reports claims by Avelino Salas and Nicolás Rodríguez that opponents of Cárdenas were organizing and that a revolt was imminent. The writer assesses the Cárdenas government as endangered by economic crisis and discusses several possible modes of regime change.

subfiles.title: File note on Dr. S. Mikesell's allegations of Japanese influence
subfiles.about: The note indexes a letter blaming Mexican conduct on Japanese influence and promises of military and economic aid.
subfiles.summary: Mikesell praised Secretary Hull's position in a contemporary dispute with Mexico. He attributed Mexico's actions to purported Japanese offers of military and naval power, supplies, and commercial products.

subfiles.title: File note on James A. Farley's report of Japanese inroads
subfiles.about: The note refers to a letter from James A. Farley reporting Mr. Jones's statements about Japanese inroads in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This is an administrative index to correspondence filed elsewhere under 812.154/319. It records the subject without reproducing the underlying allegations.

subfiles.title: Restricted memorandum on a proposed Japanese-Mexican fishing concern
subfiles.about: The memorandum describes a rumored jointly controlled company intended to dominate fishing around Baja California.
subfiles.summary: It reports that Mexico was considering a company with equal Mexican and Japanese ownership but Japanese control over fishing operations. Sánchez, the former Ensenada fish-and-game chief, was said to oppose the proposal, while some officials in Mexico City had become pro-Japanese. The writer feared that the company and associated canneries could exclude American fishing and undersell American products.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting naval reports on Japanese activities
subfiles.about: The instruction transmits a fleet commander's report and an Office of Naval Intelligence memorandum on Japanese activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The embassy was given the reports confidentially and invited to comment. The enclosures were dated August 7 and August 11, 1938.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning Japanese engineers and an asbestos mine
subfiles.to: William A. Smale, American Consul, Ensenada
subfiles.about: Mooers reports that two Japanese engineers were expected to examine Alberto Moreno's asbestos mine near El Álamo.
subfiles.summary: Vice Consul Myers learned that the engineers' arrival was reportedly being arranged through the Mexican government in Mexico City. An American resident of Calexico named Grey supplied the information and a mineral sample. Mooers promised to relay any further details because the Department was monitoring Japanese activities in Mexico.

subfiles.title: File note on a possible Japanese naval or espionage base
subfiles.about: The note indexes a despatch discussing the possibility of a Japanese naval or espionage base in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report characterized the Gulf as a potential site for a Japanese naval base. It also described the area as a particularly effective hiding place for an espionage installation.

subfiles.title: File note on Mexico's restrictions on foreign fishing
subfiles.about: The note summarizes developments after Mexico ordered foreign vessels excluded from Mexican fishing waters.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report examined the effect of the order on Japanese fishing plans. It interpreted the measure as evidence of a growing anti-Japanese attitude in Mexican official circles.

subfiles.title: File note for Despatch No. 602 on Commander Dillon's visit
subfiles.about: The note indexes Yepis's report on Naval Attaché W. M. Dillon's investigation of Japanese vessels at Guaymas.
subfiles.summary: It identifies Dillon as the American Naval and Air Attaché in Mexico. The underlying despatch concerns his visit to investigate Japanese vessels and local awareness of his mission.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 602, Visit of Commander W. M. Dillon to Guaymas
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Yepis reports Japanese foreknowledge of Dillon's visit and his own exchanges with Nippon Suisan manager Gustavo Bravo.
subfiles.summary: Bravo claimed that Mexico City had warned him Dillon would investigate Japanese vessels because of reports submitted by Yepis, but Yepis treated the claim as a bluff intended to elicit information. Yepis concluded that the episode showed Japanese efforts to monitor American officials and recommended making Dillon's visit conspicuously public. He also recounts Bravo's version of a conversation between President Roosevelt and Mexican naval officer Roberto Gómez Maqueo about future difficulties with Japan. Dillon proceeded with courtesy calls in Guaymas and Hermosillo.

subfiles.title: File note for Despatch No. 600 on Japanese shrimp fleets
subfiles.about: The note summarizes the renewed operation and expansion of Japanese shrimp fleets in Mexican waters.
subfiles.summary: Two Japanese concerns were preparing seventeen vessels to sail from Guaymas, and one fleet had already caught thirty-seven tons of shrimp for transshipment through Los Angeles to Japan. Yepis could not confirm why Mexico had again permitted the activity and noted a large increase in Japanese vessels over the previous season.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 600 on Japanese fishing activities
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Yepis reports that Japanese shrimp fleets had resumed operations from Guaymas despite an earlier Mexican prohibition.
subfiles.summary: Seventeen vessels belonging to two Japanese concerns were preparing to operate, and shrimp already caught was being sent through Los Angeles to Japan. Several explanations for the Mexican government's reversal had circulated, but none had been verified. Yepis notes that the Japanese fishing fleet had increased from seven vessels in the preceding season to sixteen currently engaged in fishing, with further additions rumored.

subfiles.title: File note on Brian Coyne newspaper clippings
subfiles.about: The note records receipt of newspaper clippings containing Brian Coyne's commentary on reported conditions in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The clippings were enclosed in a letter filed under 800.20210/175. Their particular assertions are not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: File note on Mooers's letter to Commander Dillon
subfiles.about: The note indexes a letter prepared during Dillon's visit about Japanese activity in the Gulf of California and the Mexicali district.
subfiles.summary: The underlying correspondence compiled reports for the Naval Attaché. It covered Japanese activity both in the Gulf and elsewhere within the Mexicali consular district.

subfiles.title: File note for Despatch No. 7737 on Dillon's west-coast visit
subfiles.about: The note indexes Ambassador Daniels's explanation that Dillon's inquiries into Japanese fishing were not confidential.
subfiles.summary: Daniels addressed information gathered during the Naval Attaché's recent visit to Guaymas. He emphasized that there had been no secrecy surrounding the investigation.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Commander Dillon's visit to the Mexican west coast
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, United States Ambassador, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Daniels corrects possible interpretations of Yepis's account by stressing that Dillon's trip was official, authorized, and public.
subfiles.summary: The visit was made with the Mexican Secretary of National Defense's consent, and Dillon carried an introduction from Federal Game Department chief Juan Zinser. Daniels notes that Japanese fishing concessions were openly discussed in Mexico City, so Japanese awareness of the trip was unsurprising. Dillon traveled in uniform, observed diplomatic etiquette, and called on military, naval, and fisheries officials. Daniels also questions the plausibility and propriety of recording the remarks attributed to President Roosevelt in Yepis's despatch.

subfiles.title: Letter from E. L. Munch on Japanese and German activity in Mexico
subfiles.about: Munch reports rumors that Japan sought an air base and mining control in western Mexico and might cooperate with Germany.
subfiles.summary: Recalling visits to Culiacán in 1932–1933, Munch says he heard that Japan sought a Mexican west-coast foothold for a wartime air base. He also relays Dr. Munday's statements about oil expropriation, Japanese influence over mines, and a possible German-Japanese plan for invasion through Mexico. He urges protection of American interests but provides no corroborating evidence.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to E. L. Munch
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Munch's January 20 letter about conditions observed in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that Munch's comments have been noted carefully. Hamilton expresses appreciation for the spirit that prompted the letter without endorsing its allegations.

subfiles.title: File note on a Standard Oil memorandum about Japanese activities
subfiles.about: The note indexes a despatch enclosing a Standard Oil representative's memorandum on Japanese activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed memorandum was dated February 9 and prepared for the California Standard Oil Company's home office. Its contents are not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: Confidential despatch on Japanese soundings in the Gulf of California
subfiles.about: Mooers identifies former crewman Milton W. McCree as a possible source on early Japanese coastal sounding operations.
subfiles.summary: A Mexican fisherman said McCree had worked aboard a Japanese vessel in the Gulf years earlier and observed it making soundings under cover of fishing, perhaps as early as 1912. McCree reportedly possessed photographs taken aboard the vessel. Mooers suggested that he might assist further investigation.

subfiles.title: File note on pro-Japanese tendencies in Mexican fisheries administration
subfiles.about: The note indexes reporting on alleged pro-Japanese tendencies in Mexico's Department of Forestry, Hunting and Fishing.
subfiles.summary: The referenced commercial attaché report discussed the education of Mexican fisheries experts in Japan. It also concerned the use of Japanese experts in Mexico.

subfiles.title: File note on Japanese petroleum concessions
subfiles.about: The note records the Mexican economy minister's denial that Japanese interests held petroleum concessions.
subfiles.summary: The minister stated that no Mexican petroleum concessions were held by Japanese interests. He acknowledged, however, that the Compañía Petrolera Veracruzana had negotiated with Japanese parties.

subfiles.title: Naval Attaché Report No. 47-39 on Japanese petroleum activity
subfiles.from: W. M. Dillon, Naval Attaché, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Dillon forwards an oil-company official's memorandum alleging Japanese investment in Mexican petroleum and pipeline plans.
subfiles.summary: The source reported that Japan's Pacific Petroleum Company had taken over Veracruzana interests and agreed to finance Tsuru. Nippon Soda Company was said to control properties in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec and to be planning a well at Concepción. It reportedly sought a pipeline concession to Salina Cruz and was negotiating the required performance deposit.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché memorandum and clippings on Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: W. F. Freehoff, Military Attaché, Mexico City
subfiles.to: War Department and Department of State
subfiles.about: Freehoff submits Mexican newspaper clippings as evidence of Japanese commercial and industrial propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that otherwise innocuous articles were intended to publicize the virtues of the Japanese Empire. The attached pieces defend Japanese low-cost production, describe textile and artificial-fiber industries, celebrate Osaka's industrial importance, and contrast Japanese or German economic systems with conventional international commerce. Their tone is promotional rather than directly political.

subfiles.title: Navy Department transmittal of a translated Japanese study of Mexico
subfiles.from: E. B. Nixon, Commander, United States Navy
subfiles.about: Nixon forwards a partial translation of a lengthy Japanese article about conditions in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Because of the original's size, only selected portions had been translated. Nixon sent the translation and accompanying comments for whatever use the State Department considered appropriate.

subfiles.title: Investigations Made in Mexico: translated excerpts
subfiles.about: The translated Japanese survey evaluates Mexican society, Japanese immigration, natural resources, trade prospects, communism, and political organizations.
subfiles.summary: The report portrays Japanese-Mexican relations as limited but potentially advantageous and gives a state-by-state table of the Japanese population in Mexico. It assesses minerals, Kiso Tsuru's Laguna oil enterprise, fishing in the Gulf of California, and ways Japan might expand trade by exploiting Mexican anti-American sentiment and official corruption. The political sections analyze communism, the C.T.M., the Mexican Revolutionary Party, the Frente Constitucional Democrático Mexicano, the oil expropriation, and public opinion surrounding Trotsky and the Soviet Union. Several passages reveal concern that conspicuous Japanese fishing or commercial activity might alert the United States.

subfiles.title: File note on cancellation of Japanese-connected petroleum concessions
subfiles.about: The note indexes Buenrostro's statements denying Japanese oil concessions and proposing cancellation of Veracruzana's concession.
subfiles.summary: Buenrostro stated that Japanese interests held no concessions in Mexico. He added that the Mexican-owned Veracruzana company's concession would be canceled because it was selling oil to Japanese buyers.

subfiles.title: G-2 Report No. 9000 on the Compañía Mexicana de Construcciones
subfiles.from: W. F. Freehoff, Military Attaché, Mexico City
subfiles.about: The report describes a Japanese-controlled Mexican construction company and its alleged interests in salt, fishing, petroleum, waterworks, and Pacific ports.
subfiles.summary: It gives the firm's incorporation, capitalization, shareholders, directors, and biographies, asserting that several Mexican shareholders were fronts for Japan's Takenaka Komuten. The company allegedly sought expropriation and exploitation of salt works, a Magdalena Bay fishing concession, west-coast fuel supplies, and waterworks at Salina Cruz. The source claimed backing from Dámaso Cárdenas and Abelardo Rodríguez and described intense secrecy at the firm's Mexico City offices. Freehoff adds broader allegations about Japanese and German attempts to displace American interests and reports a Japanese Legation secretary's detailed knowledge of Salina Cruz harbor.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on alleged espionage by Japanese fishing crews
subfiles.about: The sheet points to Naval Attaché Report No. 60-38 on alleged espionage by crews of Japanese fishing vessels.
subfiles.summary: The original report is filed under 812.628/516. This sheet contains only the subject and bibliographic reference.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese interest in La Imperial Oil Company
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of the American Republics (Bursley)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an internal memorandum about Japanese interest in purchasing La Imperial Oil Company assets.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum considered whether the ambassador should remind Mexico of assurances from Suárez and express hope that Japanese entry into the petroleum industry would be prevented. The matter is cross-referenced to file 812.6363/5901.

subfiles.title: File note on Milton J. Lindner's comments about Japanese fishing
subfiles.about: The note indexes a despatch enclosing Lindner's letter about Japanese fishing and proposed restrictive legislation.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure discussed the current position of Japanese fishing interests in Mexican waters. It also addressed legislation intended to prohibit Japanese fishing.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese oil activity in the Isthmus
subfiles.from: State Department, Division of the American Republics (Bursley)
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to reports that Japanese interests were active in the Isthmus and might receive Mexican oil concessions.
subfiles.summary: The underlying memorandum is filed under 800.20210/355. The damaged date indicates June 1939, but the precise day is unclear.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on observation trips to check Japanese activity
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to instructions for United States officers to make observation trips in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The trips were intended to check reports of Japanese activity. The original instruction, No. 2554, is filed under 800.20210/314.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese interests in Mexican shrimp fishing
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to Lindner's letter to Charles E. Jackson about Japanese shrimp interests and possible Mexican vessel purchases.
subfiles.summary: Lindner asked about prospects for a loan enabling Mexico to purchase shrimp-fishing boats. He believed that acquisition of such boats might lead Mexico to order Japanese fleets out of its waters.

subfiles.title: File charge slip
subfiles.about: The slip records the temporary charging or circulation of file 894.20212.
subfiles.summary: It contains only a file number, abbreviated remarks, a partly legible name or notation, and a date-like entry. No substantive report appears on the page.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese activities at San Luis, Sonora
subfiles.about: Mooers reports a proposed shell-button operation at San Luis and the unexplained arrival of Ichizo Komata and four other Japanese in Mexicali.
subfiles.summary: Saburo Yoshizaki and two companions inquired about importing Japanese seashells through San Francisco and Yuma for a button factory at San Luis, Sonora. An American postmaster suspected espionage, although Mooers noted commercial reasons why the scheme might be genuine and questioned only the remote location. The despatch also records the May arrival by air of Ichizo Komata and four unidentified Japanese whose purpose and destination remained unknown. Mooers promised continued investigation of both groups.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese negotiations at Barra de Pichi
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a rumor that Japanese agents sought concessions and offered to finance a railroad from Barra de Pichi to iron deposits.
subfiles.summary: The proposed aid was linked to completion of a contemplated railroad from a port to inland iron-ore resources. The original Justice Department letter is filed under 862.20212/1795.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese land purchases and surveying in Guerrero
subfiles.about: The sheet reports that Amonaki and Ichiquito bought a farm near supposed Guerrero iron deposits and maintained surveying equipment there.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese occupants were said to possess expensive surveying and photographic apparatus. The source believed they were Japanese government agents conducting geological examinations, but the allegation is presented without corroboration.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on correspondence about Japanese activity
subfiles.about: The sheet points to Despatch No. 44 containing correspondence about Japanese activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The correspondence had also been sent recently to the Mexico City Consulate General. The original is filed under 800.20210/405.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on James A. Farley's report of Japanese inroads
subfiles.about: The sheet repeats the reference to Farley's letter reporting Mr. Jones's statements about Japanese inroads in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: It directs the reader to file 812.154/319 for the original letter. The page duplicates the subject indexed on page 15.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Nakano and Tajima's arrival in Mexico City
subfiles.about: The sheet summarizes a telegram about Japanese businessmen investigating Mexican petroleum, salt, and oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Tomonori Nakano and S. Tajima of Okura and Company arrived with Alejandro Klyeff, who was associated with Abraham Z. Phillips and an oil-export credit. Klyeff tried to charter an aircraft for Los Mochis and Ojo de Liebre before the party chose overland travel. Nakano claimed an interest in salt and petroleum industries, while the prospective oil shipments were intended for Japan or Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Nakano and Tajima's planned Poza Rica survey
subfiles.about: The sheet reports plans for Phillips, Nakano, Tajima, and Senator Dávila to survey Poza Rica by chartered aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Nakano said he had come through the United States to purchase equipment for a Japanese refinery. The embassy nevertheless believed he was interested in Mexican crude oil and possibly connected with Japanese parties involved in La Veracruzana.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on the Japanese commercial party's flight to Poza Rica
subfiles.about: The sheet lists the Japanese and Mexican party that flew from Mexico City to Poza Rica in connection with petroleum activity.
subfiles.summary: The travelers included Shigeo Tajima, Tomonori Nakano, Senator José Santos Alonso, Abraham Z. Phillips, Jaime Paira, Humberto Chona, Yukio Nagamatsu, and Alejandro Nakagawa. Tajima and Nakano had booked Pan American Airways travel to Washington for October 20, while Phillips planned to travel to Houston on October 25.
